bal0: Calf Strain and Tear: The First 72 Hours, Recovery and Exercises | İhsan Eren
bal1: A sudden, sharp pain in your calf? What to do in the first 72 hours after a calf strain, when to return to sport and how to tell it apart from a blood clot. Warning signs and six home exercises.
bal3: While running, jumping or making a sudden movement, did you feel a sharp pain in your calf, as if you had been stabbed? A calf strain happens when there is a small tear in one of the two large calf muscles. It is a common sports injury and usually settles within a few weeks. The right care in the first few days, followed by gradual exercise, speeds recovery and helps prevent another injury.

bal9: Sudden, sharp, tearing or stabbing pain at the back of the leg.
bal10: Tightness and stiffness in the calf; with a minor strain you may be able to carry on.
bal11: Swelling and bruising in the calf, which may spread towards the ankle.
bal12: Pain or difficulty standing on tiptoe; with a severe tear, putting weight on the leg is very painful.
bal13: The calf has two main muscles: the large surface muscle (gastrocnemius) and the muscle beneath it, lower down (soleus). Both join the Achilles tendon.
bal14: When the muscle is overstretched or meets a sudden, forceful load, part of it can tear.
bal15: What helps in the first few days?
bal17: Cut down your activity for the first 72 hours, but don’t rest completely. A supportive shoe with a slight heel makes walking easier.
bal18: Apply ice wrapped in a damp towel for 15–20 minutes, checking your skin every 5 minutes. Don’t put ice directly on the skin.
bal20: If there is swelling, you can use a compression bandage or sock. Keep your leg raised above heart level while resting.
bal22: For the first 72 hours, avoid heat, alcohol, running and massage. Smoking slows healing.
bal23: Six exercises to help the calf heal
bal24: Start with the first two exercises. Once the pain has settled and you no longer need crutches, move on to the stretching and strengthening exercises. Keep the movements pain-free; stop at the point of pain.
bal26: Sit or lie down. Pull your toes and ankle towards you and hold for 5 seconds, then point your foot away and hold for 5 seconds. Stay within a pain-free range.
bal27: Sit with your leg straight and loop a towel or belt around the ball of your foot. Holding the ends, pull your foot towards you until you feel a gentle stretch in your calf.
bal29: Stand facing a chair or wall. Step back with your injured leg, keeping it straight with the heel on the floor. Bend your front knee and lean forward until you feel a stretch in your calf.
bal31: Keep your injured leg slightly behind the other, with your toes pointing forward. Keeping the injured heel on the floor, bend both knees; you’ll feel the stretch lower down in the calf.
bal33: Start once you can stand on tiptoe without pain. Hold on to a chair with your weight spread evenly over both feet. Rise up onto your toes as high as you can, hold for 5 seconds and lower slowly. As it gets easier, add repetitions, then progress to one leg.
bal34: If you could stand on one leg before the injury, you can start from week 2. Holding on to something firm, stand on your injured leg; as it gets easier, try without support and, if it is safe, with your eyes closed.
bal36: How can I tell it apart from an Achilles tendon rupture?
bal37: It isn’t always easy. A “snap” above the heel, a feeling of being struck in the back of the leg, a gap in the tendon, walking flat-footed and being unable to rise onto tiptoe at all point to an Achilles tendon rupture. In that case, go to A&E without delay.
bal38: When can I return to running and sport?
bal39: Most people feel better after about 2 weeks, but avoiding strenuous exercise for up to 8 weeks is advised to reduce the risk of re-injury. Once you have full strength and movement and can walk briskly without pain or swelling, start sport-specific drills and build up your training gradually.
bal41: A compression bandage or sock on the calf can help control swelling. Take it off when you sleep. Remove it straight away if you notice tingling, numbness, a blue colour or increasing pain in your foot.
bal42: Not always; most people recover with this advice. If 10 days after the injury you still cannot put weight on your foot and your calf is painful and swollen, see a physiotherapist.
bal43: Most people feel better after about 2 weeks; recovery usually takes around 6 weeks. A severe tear can take up to 3 months to heal fully, and mild pain and swelling sometimes last 3–6 months.
